title: The Sickness from Ambalangoda: A Collector's Curse
description:
On Sri Lanka's southern coast, Ambalangoda is famed for its vibrant Sanni demon masks, traditionally carved to ward off specific diseases. But what if one of these ancient protectors becomes a source of dread?
This story, inspired by Sri Lankan folklore, explores the chilling consequences when a modern collector brings an antique Sanni mask into his home, blurring the line between art and ancient power.
fiction_note: Inspired by Sri Lankan folklore; characters and events are dramatised for storytelling.

scenes.narration: Have you ever felt a cold touch, on a humid night, when nothing is there, yet you know something unseen brushes past? The kind that makes your blood thin, a prickle on your skin? Rohan, he knew that feeling well, a premonition perhaps, even before the true strangeness began. He was a collector, you see, drawn to the raw, untamed power of Ambalangoda's masks, their stories whispering from ancient wood. He loved the salty air, the distant roar of the ocean, the unique blend of wood dust and fresh rain that clung to that coastal town. But one particular evening, in a cluttered workshop, small and hot, lit only by a single, sputtering kerosene lamp, a light that barely pushed back the encroaching darkness, he saw *it*. A mask. Unlike any other he had encountered, tucked away deep in the shadows, almost hidden.
visuals: Wide shot of a dusty, traditional mask carving workshop at dusk, open door, single kerosene lamp casting long shadows, humid atmosphere, 50mm lens.
Close-up detail of a shelf laden with various carved wooden masks, one darker and older in the back, slightly out of focus, warm low light.

scenes.narration: He pointed, his finger tracing the air towards that shadowed corner. "That one, *Seeya*," Rohan said, his voice bright with a collector's eagerness, using the respectful term for an elder. The old carver, Sunil, a man whose hands were gnarled and scarred from decades of shaping wood, looked up slowly from a half-finished piece. His eyes, dark as polished ebony and heavy with years, lingered on the mask Rohan indicated. A deep sigh escaped him. "Ah, that one, mahattaya... it is not for sale. It... it carries old energies, potent ones. It is not like the others you see here, merely carved for display. This is a *Kana Sanniya* mask, the demon of blindness. A very powerful one." His voice was low, almost a whisper, as if the very mention of its name was a risk.
visuals: Silhouette of an older man, Sunil, back to camera, working on a mask with a chisel in the dim, smoky light of a workshop, humid air. Shot from a low angle.
Rohan's hand, blurred in the foreground, reaching towards a dark, heavy, ancient wooden mask resting on a rough wooden table, the mask's empty eye sockets prominent.

scenes.narration: Rohan, though, possessed the single-minded persistence of a true collector. He heard not a warning in Sunil's words, but a thrilling challenge, an opportunity to possess something truly unique. He pressed, his voice firm, then offered a sum that made Sunil's dark eyes widen, a sum far beyond what a piece of old, unpolished wood should ever fetch. The old man was silent for a long, heavy moment, the only sound the distant croak of a gecko. Finally, he sighed, a sound laden with deep resignation, as if giving away a secret. "Take it then, mahattaya," Sunil said, his voice barely audible. "But remember, these are not mere art. They have a purpose, a true purpose. Don't just hang it like a painting in your fine house." Rohan nodded, already picturing its place, a triumphant centrepiece. Outside, the evening rain began, a soft, steady drumming on the corrugated iron roof.
visuals: Rohan's hands counting crisp currency notes on a worn wooden counter, Sunil's face partially obscured, looking away, a bundle wrapped in old newspaper beside the money.
Rain streaking down a dusty, grimy windowpane of the workshop, blurring the view of the street outside, reflections of flickering lamplight.

scenes.narration: Back in his modern Colombo apartment, with its sleek, minimalist decor and cool, sterile air, the space felt strangely cold, almost too quiet. Rohan carefully unwrapped the mask from its newspaper shroud. Under the bright, almost clinical recessed lights of his study, it looked profoundly different. More alive, somehow, than it had in the workshop's flickering gloom. The painted eyes, once appearing dull and ancient, now seemed to hold a sharp, unsettling intelligence, a knowing gaze that pierced the pristine white wall. He hung it proudly, centered against the stark backdrop, a triumphant, exotic addition to his carefully curated collection. But as he stepped back to admire it, a faint, almost imperceptible chill, distinct from the air conditioning, settled in the air around the mask. He shivered, dismissing it as the evening breeze from the balcony.
visuals: A sleek, modern apartment living room at night, the ancient, dark wooden mask starkly contrasting against a bright, minimalist white wall, cool artificial light, 24mm lens.
Close-up detail of the mask's painted, wide-open eyes, appearing to stare directly forward, intricate carvings, shadows playing on its features under a sharp, artificial light.

scenes.narration: The first subtle signs began that very night. A faint, metallic tang in the air, a scent he couldn't quite place, hung heavy in his apartment, even with the windows closed. He saw fleeting peripheral movement, shadows dancing at the edge of his vision, vanishing the instant he turned his head. He found himself unusually, profoundly tired, a dull, insistent ache throbbing behind his eyes, a heavy weight pressing down on his eyelids. He tried to blame it on the long drive back from Ambalangoda, the sheer excitement of his new acquisition. But each time he walked past the study, the mask seemed to draw his gaze, its dark, carved surface appearing distinctly colder, somehow, than the room’s ambient temperature. A prickle of unease, a shiver completely unrelated to the air conditioning, traced its way down his spine.
visuals: Rohan's silhouette by a large, rain-streaked apartment window, looking out at a hazy, distant city skyline, a faint, distorted reflection of the mask visible in the glass behind him, 85mm lens.
A flickering table lamp on a modern desk, casting dancing, erratic shadows on the mask's carved, unmoving face on the wall, highlighting its features.

scenes.narration: The dull ache behind his eyes intensified, a constant pressure that never relented. Soon after, a persistent, dry cough developed, a rasping sound that tightened his chest, making each breath a shallow, painful effort. Sleep offered no escape; instead, he was plagued by vivid, unsettling dreams. Always the same: a shadowy figure, its eyes hollow and unseeing, reaching, always reaching for him from the oppressive darkness. He felt a pervasive weakness, a debilitating chill that seemed to seep into his very bones, despite the thick, humid Colombo air. Doctors ran tests, baffled, finding nothing medically wrong. He stopped looking directly at the mask, the thought of its gaze a torment, but his eyes were always drawn to its periphery, feeling its cold presence even when his back was turned. Sleep became a nightly battle, his body aching, his mind restless and terrified.
visuals: Rohan lying in bed, bathed in the dim, cool blue light filtering from a distant city through his window, his face drawn and pale, 35mm lens.
The mask, now appearing slightly out of focus in the background of the study, seeming to peer from the deep shadows, its features indistinct but menacing.

scenes.narration: One morning, a wave of dizziness hit him with such force, the room spun violently, and he stumbled, crashing against the doorframe, gasping for air. He knew, with a horrifying, undeniable certainty, it was the mask. It had to be. He had to move it, had to get it out of his home, out of his life. He approached the study, his heart hammering against his ribs like a frantic drum. He lifted his hand, fingers trembling uncontrollably, aiming for the carved edge of the mask. But a strange, unseen resistance held him back, an inexplicable weakness flooding his limbs, paralyzing him. His hands shook violently, independently of his will. He couldn't bring himself to touch it. He felt utterly watched, trapped in his own home. His reflection in the glass of a framed photograph on the opposite wall seemed distorted, his eyes wide with a terror he barely recognised as his own.
visuals: Rohan's trembling hand reaching towards the mask on the wall, but not quite touching it, blurred in the extreme foreground, focus on the mask, 100mm macro lens.
A wide shot of the study, Rohan standing unnaturally still, back to camera, facing the mask on the wall, appearing rigid and powerless, cold light.

scenes.narration: Desperation, cold and sharp, clawed at him, a physical ache in his chest. He remembered Sunil's last, ominous words, echoing in his fevered mind: "Don't just hang it, mahattaya. They have a purpose." Frantically, his trembling fingers fumbled for his phone, searching for the old carver's contact, only to find the number disconnected, lost to time. He spent endless hours hunched over his laptop, his eyes burning, searching for "Sanni masks," "Ambalangoda rituals," anything that might offer an explanation, a solution. He found obscure old articles, academic papers discussing their profound spiritual purpose, their ancient, intricate rituals, never their aesthetic value. They weren't just art; they were conduits, powerful containers, meant to hold or dispel specific afflictions. The relentless rain outside, a thick curtain of grey, mirrored the storm raging in his mind, each thud against the glass amplifying his mounting dread, his crushing isolation.
visuals: Rohan's face illuminated by the harsh glow of a laptop screen in a dark room, his eyes wide and fearful, rain streaking the window behind him, 50mm lens.
A close-up of an old, weathered book open to an illustration of an intricate Sanni mask ritual, blurred Sinhala text surrounding the drawing, sepia tones.

scenes.narration: Through a distant, almost forgotten contact – an old university professor who remembered Rohan’s youthful enthusiasm for folklore – he finally found a *gurunnanse*, a traditional healer, living in a quiet, unassuming inland village. The *gurunnanse* arrived late that night, a small, wiry man with eyes that seemed to see everything, yet expressed nothing. He carried only a simple, worn cloth bag, smelling faintly of dried herbs and woodsmoke. He walked into the modern apartment, his steps silent, paused, and without a single word, his gaze, calm and knowing, fell directly upon the mask on the wall. A long, heavy silence stretched between the three men, broken only by the incessant drumming of rain outside. He shook his head slowly, a deep, sorrowful sigh escaping his lips. "This one, mahattaya..." he murmured, his voice soft but resonant, "it wants to finish its work."
visuals: An old *gurunnanse*, back to camera, entering Rohan's modern apartment, holding a small cloth pouch, the mask visible on the distant wall, framed in the doorway, 35mm lens.
The *gurunnanse*'s weathered hand gesturing subtly towards the mask, a look of solemn understanding and concern on his face, shot from a respectful side angle, soft lamp light.

scenes.narration: The *gurunnanse* spoke softly, his voice a calm counterpoint to Rohan’s racing heart, explaining the true, terrifying nature of the mask. It was carved, he said, to contain the affliction of *Kana Sanniya*, the demon of blindness itself, meant to draw the sickness, the 'sanniya', from the afflicted and hold it captive. But this particular mask, he explained, was either stolen from its proper place, or perhaps never fully blessed, or its intricate ritual deliberately left incomplete. Whatever the reason, it held the 'sanniya' within it, dormant, yes, but undeniably alive, waiting. And Rohan, in his profound ignorance, had brought it into his home, given it a new, vulnerable host. It wasn't just a piece of art; it was a hungry, potent spirit, seeking to complete its purpose. It had to be returned, he insisted, given its true purpose, its true resting place.
visuals: Rohan sitting on the floor, head bowed, looking up at the *gurunnanse* who stands solemnly before the mask, arms folded, the mask dominating the frame above them, low angle.
A wide shot of the apartment's study at dawn, the mask now visible in the cool natural light, appearing more stark and sinister on the wall, its empty eyes catching the light.

scenes.narration: Weakened and profoundly shaken, Rohan, looking utterly spent, followed the *gurunnanse* back to Ambalangoda the next morning. The coastal air, once so pleasant, now felt heavy with unspoken stories. Sunil, the old carver, saw them approach his workshop and merely nodded slowly, a look of weary recognition in his deep-set eyes, as if he had always known this day would come. He took the mask back without a single word, his touch gentle, almost reverent. A small, quiet ritual was performed right there in the dusty workshop, whispers of ancient Pali and Sinhala prayers mingling with the sweet, acrid smoke of incense swirling around the dark, ancient wood. Rohan felt a lightness, a profound release, return to his body almost immediately. He recovered slowly, but the memory, the terrifying cold touch, the hollow-eyed dreams, lingered like a deep, persistent chill in his very bones. He never collected masks again. The old people, they say, some things are best left to their true purpose, undisturbed.
visuals: Rohan, looking pale but relieved, handing the now wrapped mask back to Sunil in the traditional workshop, both men's faces solemn, early morning light filtering in.
A final shot of the mask, now placed reverently on a high, shadowed shelf in the workshop, obscured by other carvings, a single oil lamp burning nearby, its flame casting a soft, protective glow.

shorts.title: He Thought It Was Art... Then The Sickness Began.
shorts.narration: Rohan, an antique collector, found a rare Sanni demon mask in Ambalangoda. The old carver warned him, "It carries old energies. Not like the others." Rohan, captivated by its ancient power, ignored the cryptic words, dismissing them as superstitious folklore. He paid a hefty sum, convinced he'd found a masterpiece for his collection. Back in his sleek Colombo apartment, the mask looked even more striking, its painted eyes unsettlingly intense. But soon, a dull ache started behind his eyes. Then a cough, persistent and dry. His strength began to wane. He felt constantly cold, despite the humid air. He thought it was stress, or a simple flu. But the mask... it felt like it was watching him. The full story is on our channel.

shorts.title: The Mask Wouldn't Let Him Go.
shorts.narration: The illness grew worse. Rohan's body ached, his mind plagued by unsettling dreams. He knew, with a horrifying certainty, it was the mask. He had to get rid of it. He walked into his study, his heart pounding, his limbs heavy. He reached out a trembling hand, aiming for its carved edge. But a strange, invisible force pushed back. A sudden, profound weakness overwhelmed him, paralyzing his muscles. His fingers shook violently, unable to complete the simple act. He couldn't touch it. He was trapped, bound by something ancient and malevolent. The mask had claimed its space, and now, it wouldn't let him go. The full story is on our channel.
